food.text: Farming reached Iran very early. Agriculture first appeared there some 12,000 years ago, at about the same time as the better-documented settlements of the Fertile Crescent.
At Ganj Dareh, in the central Zagros Mountains of western Iran, the oldest settlement remains date back to c. 8200 BC. They have yielded the earliest evidence for goat domestication in the world.
Agriculture first appeared in Iran some 12,000 years ago, alongside better-documented settlements in the Fertile Crescent. The Chogha Golan site featured early domestication of emmer wheat.

The Shulaveri–Shomu people were proficient farmers who kept goat, sheep, cow, pig and dog from the earliest phase. Their crops included 10 species of wheat, several types of barley, lentil, pea, cultivated grape and melon. The culture covered parts of northern Iran.
The Chogha Golan site in Iran featured early domestication of emmer wheat. It shows that people in the region were shaping wild grain into a farmed crop very early.
The site of Ganj Dareh features the earliest known domestication of goats, around 10,000 years ago. It is a contemporary of the Chogha Golan site, where early farming in Iran also took place.
Some of the oldest agricultural ground has been discovered at Susa and at Chogha Mish, a settlement dating back to 6800 BC. Both places lie in the south-western part of Iran.

In the eighth millennium BC, agricultural communities such as Chogha Bonut, the earliest village in Susiana, started to form in western Iran. This happened either through indigenous development or through outside influences.

In the eighth millennium BC, agricultural communities began to form in western Iran, perhaps through indigenous development or outside influences. One of them, Chogha Bonut, was the earliest village in Susiana.

art.text: More than 50,000 pieces of prehistoric rock art have been discovered in Iran. Dating back 7000 years before present, rock art is the oldest surviving artwork in the country.
The earliest known clay vessels and modeled human and animal terracotta figurines in Iran were produced around the eighth millennium BC. They came from Ganj Dareh and Tepe Sarab in western Iran.
Evidence of a painted-pottery civilization around Susa has been dated to about 5000 BCE. Susa later fell firmly within the Sumerian Uruk cultural sphere.

The ibex, a goat with prominent curved horns, is the most common image in Iranian rock art. Human figures appear too, dressed and undressed, performing rituals, roping cattle, walking, riding horses and hunting.

The earliest known petroglyphs in Iran are at Teimareh, near Golpayegan County, and date back 7000 years. The largest rock art panel in Iran, near Golpayegan, spans 12 meters and features more than 100 petroglyphs.

Shortly after Susa was first settled 6000 years ago, its inhabitants erected a temple on a monumental platform. The ceramic vessels were placed as offerings in a thousand or more graves near the base of the platform, and nearly two thousand pots were recovered from this cemetery, most now in the Louvre. Many were a drinking goblet, a serving dish and a small jar, implying food and drink, apparently thought as necessary for life in the afterworld as in this one. Plainer cooking-type jars and bowls were probably the grave goods of humbler citizens as well as adolescents and, perhaps, children.

The earliest known clay vessels and modeled human and animal terracotta figurines were produced at Ganj Dareh in western Iran. There are also 10,000-year-old human and animal figurines from Tepe Sarab in Kermanshah Province.
Archaeologists classify the tools used to carve petroglyphs by their historical era. Incising tools include flint, metal, or the thigh bones of hunted prey.

Ancient Iranian pottery and bronze sculpture continue designs found in the rock art. This continuity can be traced from the eighth millennium BC in the pottery of Ganj Dareh, suggesting that rock carvings impressed ancient Iranian artisans.

At Ganj Dareh, clay was used for figurines and small geometric pieces like cones and disks, dated to about 7300-6900 BC. A second tradition used clay for mud-walled buildings around 7300 BC. Both traditions are shared with Tepe Guran and Tepe Sarab.

According to Catherine Marro (2022), the systematic use of chaff, creating a Chaff-Faced Ware effect, is attested from the beginning of the 5th millennium BCE. It developed together with the Dalma culture.

science.text: Ganj Dareh, a Neolithic settlement in the Zagros Mountains, has yielded the earliest evidence for goat domestication in the world. Its oldest remains date to about 8200 BC. The only domesticated crop found there so far is two-row barley.

The Sialk Ziggurat, a monumental stepped platform built around 3000 BCE, is arguably the oldest ziggurat in the world. Excavations from 1999 to 2004 revealed it was built with approximately 1.25 million mud bricks.

Before writing, people used clay tokens as an early predecessor to it. About 135 tokens, in shapes including small cones, spheres and discs, were found at Chogha Mish. Tokens like these were enclosed in hollow clay envelopes called bullae, and at least 28 envelopes with seal impressions were also found.
Combs have been used since prehistoric times. Very refined examples have been discovered in settlements in Persia dating back 5,000 years.
Tepe Yahya was a site of early metallurgy. Four metal artifacts were found there, including a copper shaft-hole axe from layer IVB5 and a copper spearhead from layer IVC2.

More than 1,000 steatite pieces from Period IVB at Tepe Yahya point to local manufacturing, and a steatite mine was found near the site. Steatite vessels made there have turned up in Mesopotamia, Bampur, Shahr-e Sukhteh and even lower levels at Mohenjodaro in India.

Ganj Dareh shows two early ceramic traditions. One used clay for figurines and small geometric pieces like cones and disks, dated to about 7300 to 6900 BC. The other used clay for mud-walled buildings, from about 7300 BC.
A copper and lead figurine from Tepe Yahya contains 10.6% lead. This lead content shows that it actually dates from the Late Uruk period.

In the late 4th millennium BC, a monumental building covered the top of the Tepe Yahya mound. It used a standardized brick measuring 48 x 24 x 8 centimeters. Builders worked from a base measure of 72 cm, approximating the large cubit used across the ancient Near East.

Around 3000 BC, potters at Shahr-e Sukhteh reproduced ceramic styles from Turkmenistan, 750 km to the north. Other ceramics were imported from the Kech-Makran area and from the Mundigak region in Afghanistan.

Tall-e Bakun had large workshop areas, pointing to local industry. Its people obtained goods such as shells, copper, steatite, lapis and turquoise through trade with distant regions, and the settlement was arranged according to its functional needs.

politics.text: Elam is described as emerging as a state founded in 4000 BC. It later had Susa as its capital, so one of the earliest states in the region grew up in the west of what is now Iran.

Iran is home to one of the world's oldest continuous civilizations, with historical and urban settlements dating back to the 5th millennium BC. Its central region, the Iranian plateau, is now covered by modern Iran.

Dozens of prehistoric sites across the Iranian plateau point to ancient cultures and urban settlements in the fourth millennium BC. Long before any empire arose there, organized communities already dotted the highlands.
The Proto-Elamite city of Susa was founded around 4000 BC in the watershed of the river Karun. During its early history, it fluctuated between submission to Mesopotamian power and Elamite power.

Susa is one of the oldest-known settlements of Iran and of the world. Archaeologists generally perceive it as an extension of the Sumerian city-state of Uruk, which means it took in many aspects of Mesopotamian culture.

Based on C14 dating, the city of Susa may have been founded as early as 4395 BC, a time that goes beyond the age of civilization in Mesopotamia. Many archaeologists see it as an extension of the Sumerian city-state of Uruk. Later it became the capital of Elam.

The Jiroft culture in southeastern Iran, in the province of Kerman, was one of the earliest civilizations on the Iranian plateau. Archaeological excavations there uncovered 4th-millennium BC objects, including the world's earliest known inscription.

culture.text: Jars of wine about 7,000 years old have been excavated in the Zagros Mountains, and they are now on display at the University of Pennsylvania. Ruins of 7,000-year-old settlements such as Tepe Sialk also testify to village life in this era.

Susa is one of the oldest-known settlements of Iran and the world, and it was possibly first founded as early as 4395 BC. Archaeologists generally see it as an extension of the Sumerian city-state of Uruk, so it took on many aspects of Mesopotamian culture.

Dalma pottery appeared in north-western Iran in the sixth millennium BC and spread widely in the fifth. It stayed in use until the fourth millennium BC. Jars, beakers and bowls are among the excavated Dalma vessels, and pottery is the best-understood part of the culture.
The Shulaveri–Shomu culture, present in parts of northern Iran, left anthropomorphic figurines of mainly seated women. They may have been used for religious purposes relating to a fertility cult.

The Kura–Araxes culture began about 4000 BC and stretched into northwestern Iran. Its people lived by a sedentary agricultural economy. One local variant is named the Yanik Tepe culture, after a site in Iranian Azerbaijan near Lake Urmia.

Cylinder seals from Susa in the Uruk period have a rich iconography that particularly emphasizes scenes of everyday life. Some show a local potentate whom P. Amiet sees as a proto-royal figure, preceding the priest-kings of Late Uruk.

Excavations at Dalma Tepe in 1961, part of the Hasanlu Project of the University of Pennsylvania, uncovered architectural, burial and ceramic remains. Dalma Tepe is one of the first sedentary settlements in the Ushun-Solduz Valley in north-western Iran.

Early Shulaveri–Shomu communities had very few ceramic vessels, and those were imported from Mesopotamia. Local pottery production began around 5800 BC, with handmade pots that had engraved decorations and were made from local clay.

The Kura–Araxes culture, dated to circa 3400 BC to ca. 2000 BC, stretched from northwestern Iran into the neighbouring regions of the Caucasus and Anatolia. Its reach shows that early societies linked northwestern Iran to lands well beyond the plateau.

Catherine Marro (2022) notes that the systematic use of chaff in pottery, creating a Chaff-Faced Ware effect, is attested from the beginning of the 5th millennium BCE with the development of the Dalma culture. Chaff-faced ware also appeared in the South Caucasus and Upper Mesopotamia.
